text.en: In January 1755 Moscow University was founded; that November an earthquake destroyed Lisbon and shook all of Europe.
Steller's sea cow was discovered in 1741 and wiped out in just 27 years: the last was apparently killed in 1768, the year Cook set off on his first voyage.
In January 1775 Pugachev was executed in Moscow; in April the first shots of the American War of Independence were fired.
The Bolshoi Theatre and the United States are the same age: the theatre dates from March 1776, the Declaration of Independence from July of that year.
Antarctica was first sighted only in 1820, by the Bellingshausen–Lazarev expedition — by then Watt's steam engine was already half a century old.
Two months before Waterloo, in April 1815, Indonesia's Tambora erupted — its ash brought the 'Year Without a Summer' to Europe and North America.
In May 1844 Morse sent the first telegram from Washington to Baltimore; ten days later the last pair of great auks was killed in Iceland.
The brutal winter of 1709, the 'Great Frost', struck all of Europe and wore down Charles XII's Swedish army before Poltava.
Moscow University was founded in January 1755. That November an earthquake destroyed Lisbon and shook the philosophers of the Enlightenment.
Catherine II corresponded with Voltaire and Diderot and offered to publish the Encyclopédie, banned in France, in Riga.
1825: the first public steam railway opened in England, and in St Petersburg the Decembrists marched onto Senate Square.
1804: Napoleon crowned himself emperor, while the former slaves of Haiti, having beaten his army, declared independence — the first nation founded by a slave revolt.

The pirate republic in the Bahamas was ended by the man who rescued the real Robinson Crusoe. Woodes Rogers took Alexander Selkirk off his desert island in 1709 and became governor of the Bahamas in 1718.
Blackbeard held the people of a whole city hostage — and asked for a chest of medicine. Once he got it, he released his captives and lifted the blockade of Charleston in May 1718.
History's most famous pirate was a pirate for only about two years. Blackbeard appears in records in 1716 and died in 1718 — and there is no reliable account of him killing anyone he held captive.
Pirates had their own injury insurance. Crew articles set in advance how much a man would get for losing an arm or a leg in battle — and the captain was chosen by vote.

Two women pirates escaped the gallows because they were pregnant. Anne Bonny and Mary Read of Calico Jack's crew were sentenced to death in 1720 but reprieved; Read died in prison, Bonny's fate is unknown.
The Koh-i-Noor diamond is said to have been named by Nader Shah. Seeing it after the sack of Delhi in 1739, he reportedly cried out "Koh-i-Noor!" — "Mountain of Light".
In 1726 a surgeon to the royal household believed an Englishwoman was giving birth to rabbits. Mary Toft fooled doctors for weeks before confessing in London.

Isaac Newton lost a fortune in a stock bubble. He is said to have lost about £20,000 in the South Sea Company in 1720, remarking that he could calculate the motions of heavenly bodies but not the madness of people.
Britain and Spain fought for nine years over a severed ear. Spaniards cut off Captain Jenkins's ear in 1731; after he told Parliament about it, war broke out in 1739.
The Vatican forbade copying Allegri's Miserere, but 14-year-old Mozart wrote it down from memory. His father said one hearing in the Sistine Chapel in 1770 was enough.
The navy's most famous mutiny broke out on a ship carrying plants. The Bounty was taking breadfruit seedlings from Tahiti to the West Indies when its crew rose up in 1789.
Captain Bligh, set adrift by mutineers, sailed 6,700 km in an open boat. He had 18 men, few supplies and almost no charts, and reached Timor in 47 days.
The Bounty mutineers' hideout was found only 18 years later. In 1808 American sealers landed on Pitcairn and found one surviving mutineer living with the others' children.

In 1795 cavalry captured a navy. Dutch warships were frozen in at Den Helder, and French hussars rode up across the ice — 14 ships surrendered without a fight. Dutch historians, though, call it more a parley than a charge.
Hawaii was first called the Sandwich Islands — after the same earl as the sandwich. In 1778 Cook named them for the First Lord of the Admiralty, the Earl of Sandwich.
Sweden once had a 30 February. Its botched switch to the new calendar ended with a return to the old one, and an extra day was added in 1712.
Britain's tax year starts on 6 April because of the 1752 calendar reform. Eleven days were dropped, so the old New Year of 25 March shifted to 5 April, and later one day more.
The Mughal emperor Aurangzeb, who ruled almost all of India, wanted his burial paid for with money earned sewing caps and copying the Quran. His simple grave lies open to the sky.
The Chinese emperor Qianlong abdicated so as not to reign longer than his grandfather. In 1795 he stepped down after 60 years out of respect for Kangxi, who had ruled for 61.
Anders Celsius designed his scale upside down: water boiled at 0 degrees and froze at 100. It was flipped only after his death.
Edmond Halley predicted that a comet would return in 1758 but did not live to see it. He died in 1742; the comet came back on schedule and was named after him.

A former prisoner of war made potatoes popular in France. Parmentier ate them in Prussian captivity during the Seven Years' War and, legend says, had soldiers guard his potato field by day so Parisians would steal from it at night.
No one sits on the Ashanti kingdom's sacred throne. Legend says the Golden Stool descended from the sky to the first king around 1701 and holds the soul of the nation.
In 1734 a man from Ghana earned a doctorate in Germany. Anton Wilhelm Amo had been given as a child to the Duke of Brunswick — and went on to teach philosophy at Halle and Jena.
Voltaire got rich by beating the state lottery. In 1729 he and the mathematician La Condamine spotted a flaw in its rules and bought up tickets until they had made a fortune.
George I liked Handel's Water Music so much he had it played three times in a row. In July 1717 some 50 musicians performed it on a barge following the king along the Thames.

Bach wrote a comic piece about coffee addiction. In his Coffee Cantata a father forbids his daughter coffee, and she refuses any suitor who won't let her drink it. It was performed in a Leipzig coffee house.
Winston Churchill called the Seven Years' War the first world war. Between 1756 and 1763 it was fought in Europe, North America, India, Africa and at sea.
The longitude problem that baffled astronomers was solved by a self-taught carpenter. John Harrison built precise sea clocks, but had to fight for the 1714 prize until he was almost 80.
The victor and the vanquished of Waterloo were the same age: Wellington was born on 1 May 1769, Napoleon on 15 August that same year.
Napoleon's Hundred Days actually lasted 110, from his return to Paris on 20 March 1815 to Louis XVIII's restoration on 8 July.
The land Napoleon sold the US in 1803 now lies in 15 American states and two Canadian provinces. It cost less than three cents an acre.

Admiral Nelson's body came home from Trafalgar in a cask of brandy. There was no lead aboard for a coffin, so the surgeon used the largest water cask, which had to be topped up with spirits several times on the way.
'The Congress dances, but it does not move forward,' went the joke about the Congress of Vienna: while diplomats spent months carving up post-Napoleonic Europe, Vienna went from ball to ball.

The same rainy summer of 1816 that produced Frankenstein also gave birth to the aristocratic vampire, ancestor of Dracula. Byron's doctor John Polidori wrote The Vampyre, and in 1819 it was printed under Byron's own name by mistake.

Beethoven never heard the ovation at the premiere of his Ninth Symphony. The nearly deaf composer was still beating time, and the singer Caroline Unger reportedly turned him round so he could see the applause.

Before the railways, Bristol kept its own time, ten minutes behind London. Train timetables changed that: the Great Western Railway adopted London time in 1840, and the Bristol Exchange clock still has two minute hands.
The word 'dinosaur' is younger than photography: the daguerreotype was unveiled in 1839, while Richard Owen coined the 'terrible lizard' only in 1842.

The first person ever photographed got into the picture because he was having his boots shined. In Daguerre's 1838 shot a busy Paris boulevard looks empty: the exposure took minutes, so only those standing still were caught.

The first computer program was written by Lord Byron's daughter in 1843, about a century before the first computers. Ada Lovelace showed how Babbage's engine could compute Bernoulli numbers; the machine itself was never built.
The artist of The Great Wave went by at least thirty names in his lifetime, more than any other major Japanese artist of his day. 'Hokusai' is just the best known.
England's first Indian restaurant opened in London in 1810. Its owner, Sake Dean Mahomed, later ran 'shampooing' vapour baths in Brighton and became shampooing surgeon to two kings.

Britain is the only country whose stamps carry no country name. It goes back to the world's first stamp, the 1840 Penny Black: there were no others, so no need to say where it was from. The monarch's head does the job.

Heinrich Heine coined 'Lisztomania' in 1844. Fans of Franz Liszt fought over his gloves and handkerchiefs, collected his coffee dregs, and one lady set a cigar stub he had tossed away in a diamond locket.

Darwin ate a new species before realising it was one. On the Beagle voyage his companions shot a rhea and had it for dinner; only then did he see it was the elusive lesser rhea, later named Darwin's rhea.
Abraham Lincoln is the only US president to hold a patent. In 1849 he patented a device to float riverboats over shoals; it never went into use.
In Australia a camel shot its owner. In 1846 the pack of Harry the camel, kneeling down, caught the trigger of explorer John Horrocks's gun; Horrocks died of the wound, having ordered the camel shot.
Mexico's General Santa Anna buried his own leg with full military honours. He lost it in 1838 in the Pastry War, to French grapeshot near Veracruz.

Pushkin's great-grandfather came to Russia as a boy, a 'gift' for Peter I. African-born Abram Gannibal became the tsar's godson, a military engineer and a general — and his great-grandson Russia's greatest poet.

The Hermitage cats are older than the Hermitage. In 1745 Empress Elizabeth had the best mousers brought from Kazan to the Winter Palace; Catherine II bought the paintings that began the museum only in 1764.

Russia's Students' Day is St Tatiana's Day because Elizabeth signed the decree founding Moscow University on that day in 1755 — which was also the name day of the mother of its co-founder Ivan Shuvalov.
The founder of Moscow University walked to Moscow. In 1730 the 19-year-old son of a northern fisherman set off on foot to 'study sciences'; 25 years later Mikhail Lomonosov co-founded the university.

Lomonosov discovered the atmosphere of Venus. Watching its 1761 transit across the Sun, he saw a glowing rim and correctly blamed refraction in an atmosphere. In 2012 the observation was repeated with antique telescopes.
Empress Elizabeth of Russia left behind some 15,000 dresses and several thousand pairs of shoes. She also effectively abolished the death penalty — a rarity in the 18th century.
Catherine the Great was born Princess Sophie of Anhalt-Zerbst in the Prussian port of Stettin, now Szczecin in Poland. She came to Russia at 15 and went on to rule it for 34 years.
Catherine II bought the hard-up Diderot's library, let him keep the books, made him their salaried librarian — and paid his salary 50 years in advance.

While the Thunder Stone for the Bronze Horseman was being hauled to the Neva, Cook was charting Australia. He landed at Botany Bay in April 1770, and that same year the 1,500-tonne boulder reached Saint Petersburg.

The Orthodox emperor Paul I became Grand Master of the Catholic Knights of Malta: in 1798, after Napoleon seized their island, the knights in Saint Petersburg elected the Russian tsar head of the order.

Count Fyodor Tolstoy so exasperated Krusenstern on Russia's first voyage round the world that he was put ashore in Kamchatka — after teaching the ship's orangutan to pour ink over the captain's log. He came home tattooed and nicknamed 'the American'.
Russia's fort in California was dedicated four days after Borodino. Fort Ross opened on 11 September 1812 (New Style), Alexander I's name day — and three days later Napoleon entered Moscow.
Kutuzov never wore an eye patch. In 1774 near Alushta a bullet went through his temple and out by his right eye; the eye was left squinting but intact. The black patch is a later myth.
In 1817 Russia had forts both in California and in Hawaii: Fort Ross north of San Francisco and Fort Elizabeth on Kauai. The Hawaiian one flew the Russian flag for less than a year.
Pushkin died after a duel in early 1837; that October Russia's first train ran from Saint Petersburg to Tsarskoye Selo, the town where he had gone to school.

Dostoevsky was sentenced to be shot and reprieved at the last moment. In December 1849 the first three prisoners already faced the firing squad when the sentence was commuted to hard labour. He later retold the scene in The Idiot.
Russia's fort in California was bought by John Sutter — the man whose sawmill started the Gold Rush. He acquired Fort Ross in 1841, and in 1848 gold was found at his mill.

Blackbeard and Isaac Newton were contemporaries. When the pirate was killed off North Carolina in 1718, Newton was running the Royal Mint and the Royal Society — and had more than eight years still to live.

British Australia exists partly because of American independence. Convicts used to be shipped to America; having lost it, Britain sent the First Fleet, which reached Sydney in January 1788, four months after the US Constitution was signed.

The oldest surviving photograph is only a year or two younger than the Decembrist revolt. Niépce shot the view from his window in 1826 or 1827; the exposure took anywhere from hours to days, by various estimates.
Bangkok is a younger capital than the United States is a country: King Rama I moved Siam's capital to the east bank of the Chao Phraya in 1782, six years after the Declaration of Independence.
Modern Singapore is younger than the Battle of Waterloo: Stamford Raffles set up the British trading post there in 1819, four years after Napoleon's defeat.

The Communist Manifesto and the California Gold Rush began within weeks of each other: gold was found at Sutter's Mill on 24 January 1848, and Marx and Engels's manifesto came out in London that February.

One of Europe's last 'witches' was executed 30 years after Franklin caught lightning with a kite. Anna Göldi was beheaded in Glarus, Switzerland, in 1782; Franklin described his kite experiment in 1752.

In 1749 fashionable Parisian ladies wore their hair à la rhinocéros. The cause was Clara, a rhino whom a Dutch captain toured around Europe for 17 years, from Berlin and Vienna to Versailles and Venice.

Bach wrote a musical comedy about a coffee addict. In the Coffee Cantata a father won’t let his daughter marry unless she quits coffee; she agrees, then secretly lets it be known that any suitor must allow coffee in the marriage contract.
France banned growing potatoes in 1748, believing they caused leprosy. The Paris Faculty of Medicine declared them edible only in 1772, after Parmentier’s campaign.
Russians once rioted over potatoes. In the 1840s state peasants in the Urals and Volga region rose against orders to plant potatoes on communal fields, unrest remembered as the “potato riots”.
In the 18th century Britons’ sugar intake more than quadrupled, from about 4 lb a year per person in 1700 to about 18 lb in 1800. Sweet tea, sugared by the colonies, became a working-class habit.

The hand-cranked ice-cream freezer was invented by Nancy Johnson of Philadelphia in 1843: a bucket of ice, a paddled cylinder inside and a crank. Before that it was beaten by hand for hours. She sold the patent for $200.
The mass-produced toothbrush was invented in prison. Jailed in Newgate in 1770, William Addis set bristles in a bone from his dinner; once free, by 1780 he was mass-producing toothbrushes.

Before stamps, the recipient paid for a letter, so people cheated. Rowland Hill told of a girl who glanced at an envelope from her fiancé and refused it: the news was coded on the outside. The stamp arrived in 1840.
In 1795 Britain taxed hair powder at a guinea a year. Those who paid were nicknamed “guinea pigs”, and the fashion for powdered wigs soon faded.

The sandwich is named after an earl. A French traveller claimed the Earl of Sandwich would not leave the gaming table and asked for meat between slices of bread; his biographers think he ate that way at his desk.
In Siberia, Mongolia and Tibet bricks of pressed tea served as money. They paid for goods and even taxes, and in Mongolia this tea currency stayed in use into the early 20th century.

Napoleon lost at chess to a 'robot' with a man inside. For 84 years the Mechanical Turk passed as an automaton, while strong players took turns hiding in the cabinet; Napoleon and Benjamin Franklin both played it.
Amazon Mechanical Turk is named after a chess automaton from 1770. Just like the original Turk, the 'smart machine' is really people: thousands of workers doing small tasks behind the interface.

A mechanical duck that 'digested' grain fooled audiences for over a century. Magician Jean-Eugène Robert-Houdin exposed it in 1844: the grain collected in one compartment, and pre-made 'droppings' waited in another.
The world's first car, legend says, also had the first crash. Cugnot's steam wagon, built to pull cannons, went no faster than a walk, yet in 1771 it supposedly knocked down part of a wall.

France once had clocks on which noon came at five. The Revolution split the day into 10 hours of 100 minutes, but decimal time never caught on and was dropped in 1795, while the metre and the kilogram stayed.

The metre is a slice of the Earth: one ten-millionth of the distance from the pole to the equator. Two astronomers spent six years surveying the meridian from Dunkirk to Barcelona, through revolution and war, to fix it.

Psychology has a 'Semmelweis reflex': the tendency to reject new evidence that clashes with established beliefs. It is named after the doctor whose call for handwashing saved mothers' lives and was ridiculed by his peers.

A bell in Oxford has been ringing since 1840, and nobody dares find out what powers it. Its dry piles have driven some 10 billion rings, and opening them would end one of the longest-running experiments ever.
In 1835 a New York paper 'discovered' winged people on the Moon. The Sun's hoax about lunar unicorns and bat-men sent its sales soaring, and the paper never printed a retraction.

The bicycle may owe its birth to a volcano. After Tambora erupted in 1815, Europe had its 'year without a summer' and horses died for lack of feed; one theory holds that this is why Karl Drais built his horseless running machine.

In the row over who invented calculus, Newton secretly wrote the verdict himself. The Royal Society, of which he was president, set up a committee on Leibniz's complaint in 1712, and its report in Newton's favour was drafted by Newton.

The first aeronauts were a sheep, a duck and a rooster. In September 1783 they flew in a balloon before Louis XVI at Versailles and all landed safely. The sheep was called Montauciel, 'Climb-to-the-sky'.
'What use is a newborn baby?' That, the story goes, was Benjamin Franklin's reply in Paris in 1783 when someone asked him what good a balloon could possibly be.

The word 'vaccine' comes from the Latin vacca, cow. Jenner took material from milkmaid Sarah Nelmes, who caught cowpox from a cow called Blossom. Blossom's hide still hangs in the library of St George's medical school in London.

Catherine the Great was inoculated against smallpox 28 years before Jenner's vaccine. In 1768 the English doctor Thomas Dimsdale variolated her, and the grateful empress made him a baron with a lifelong pension.

Boston learned smallpox inoculation from an enslaved African man. Onesimus told his owner, the minister Cotton Mather, that this was how people at home protected themselves, and in the 1721 epidemic the inoculated died far less often.

Anaesthesia was inspired by party tricks. People inhaled ether and laughing gas for fun at 'ether frolics', and in 1844 dentist Horace Wells noticed at one such show that a man who had gashed his leg felt no pain.
As early as 1800 Humphry Davy wrote that laughing gas might be useful in surgery. He enjoyed breathing nitrous oxide with his poet friends, but doctors ignored the hint for almost half a century.

The stethoscope was invented out of embarrassment. In 1816 doctor René Laennec felt awkward putting his ear to a young woman's chest, rolled some paper into a tube, and heard her heart better than ever before.

The man who discovered Uranus was a professional musician. William Herschel was an organist in Bath and wrote 24 symphonies, grinding telescope mirrors at night and making the best telescopes of his day.
Ketchup was once sold as medicine. In 1834 American doctor John Cook Bennett declared tomatoes a cure for diarrhoea and indigestion, and 'tomato pills' were soon on sale across the country.

The father of modern chemistry was executed as a tax collector. Lavoisier went to the guillotine in 1794 for his role in tax farming, and the mathematician Lagrange said it took a moment to cut off that head, and a century might not produce another like it.

Napoleon stood about 1.69 m, average for a Frenchman of his day. The 'short' myth came from French inches being longer than English ones, and from 'the little corporal', a term of affection rather than of size.
Marie Antoinette almost certainly never said 'Let them eat cake'. Rousseau attributed the line to 'a great princess' around 1765, when the future queen was nine and living in Vienna.
Potemkin's fake villages most likely never existed. The story of painted façades along the Dnieper was spread by the Saxon diplomat Helbig, who was not on Catherine's 1787 journey himself.

Peter the Great never spoke of cutting a 'window to Europe'. The phrase is Pushkin's, from The Bronze Horseman (1833), and as he noted himself, the image came from the Italian writer Francesco Algarotti.

Dr Guillotin did not invent the guillotine and opposed the death penalty. He only argued that, if executions were to happen, they should be equal and painless for all. He died of natural causes in 1814.
When the Bastille was stormed on 14 July 1789 it held just seven prisoners: four forgers, two lunatics and one aristocrat. The crowd was really after its stores of gunpowder.
Most delegates signed the Declaration of Independence on 2 August 1776, not 4 July. On 4 July Congress merely approved its wording.
George Washington's false teeth were not wooden. They were made of hippopotamus ivory, metal and human teeth; by his inauguration he had just one tooth of his own left.

Paul Revere never shouted 'The British are coming!' The ride was secret, British patrols were about, and colonists still saw themselves as British; witnesses recalled him saying 'The Regulars are coming out.'

Salieri did not poison Mozart. Pushkin made the rumour famous in his 1830 'little tragedy', while Salieri was a respected teacher whose pupils included Beethoven, Schubert, Liszt and Mozart's younger son.
James Watt did not invent the steam engine: Newcomen engines had been pumping mines since 1712. Watt added a separate condenser that made them far more efficient; the kettle story came later.

Schopenhauer scheduled his Berlin lectures at the very hour Hegel taught, and lost. Hundreds flocked to the famous professor; Schopenhauer drew a handful, and the next semester nobody signed up at all.

Pyotr Chaadayev was officially declared insane for writing a philosophical essay. After his Philosophical Letter appeared in 1836, Nicholas I had him pronounced mentally ill and the journal Telescope was shut down.
